visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions across week two. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: Market cap 800, debt 300, cash 100, non-controlling interests 40, a stake in an associate worth 20. Enterprise value?
questions.explain: 800 + 300 + 40 − 100 − 20 = 1,020. Non-controlling interests are added because their EBITDA is consolidated; subtracting them gives 940.
questions.explain_at: One thousand, plus four hundred, plus fifty, minus one hundred, minus fifty

questions.q: A company issues 200 of new shares and keeps the cash. What happens to enterprise value?
questions.explain: Equity value and cash both rise by 200 and cancel out. The business itself hasn't changed.
questions.explain_at: Enterprise value changes when the business changes

questions.q: Five peers trade at 6x, 7x, 8x, 9x and 25x EBITDA. Which multiple do you apply?
questions.explain: The 25x outlier drags the average up to 11x. Bankers use the median, which here is 8x.

questions.q: The unaffected share price is 20 and the offer is 26. What's the premium?
questions.explain: 26 ÷ 20 − 1 = 30%. Dividing the 6 by the offer price gives 23%, a common slip.
questions.explain_at: Two euros sixty over ten. Twenty-six percent

questions.q: PTC: about $22.6bn of equity value and $23.7bn of enterprise value. What does the gap tell you?

options.text: A premium of about $1.1bn over market value
Net debt and other claims of about $1.1bn
Cash of about $1.1bn more than its debt

questions.explain: Enterprise value is above equity value, so PTC has more debt and other claims than cash. Net cash would put enterprise value below equity value, as at Activision.
questions.explain_at: PTC has more debt and other claims than cash
